headline: PSA Finds No Matching Civil Records for 1,685 Names in Duterte Fund Lists; Defense Says They Were Aliases
seoTitle: PSA: 1,685 Duterte Fund Payee Names Had No Civil Records | FMB News
seoDescription: PSA testimony found no matching civil records for 1,685 names checked from OVP and DepEd confidential-fund lists. Duterte's defense said the names were aliases.
deck: A PSA official testified that 1,685 of 2,669 names checked from OVP and DepEd confidential-fund payee lists had no matching civil records. The defense says the names were aliases; the testimony alone does not prove any payee was fictitious.
author: FMB News Desk

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: Philippine Statistics Authority Assistant National Statistician Marizza Grande testified before the Senate impeachment court on September 7 that the agency found no matching birth, marriage or death records for 1,685 names submitted for verification from confidential-fund payee lists of the Office of the Vice President and Department of Education under Vice President Sara Duterte.

According to the Philippine News Agency, the 1,685 names comprised 1,287 from an OVP list of 1,992 names and 398 from a DepEd list of 677 names. The prosecution also presented PSA results showing that some names matched records of deceased people or minors.

Duterte defense lawyer Justin Gular later told the impeachment court that the recipient names were aliases. News5 and GMA News separately reported the defense position. The defense said it would present its evidence at the appropriate stage of the trial.

sections.heading: What the evidence does — and does not — establish
paragraphs: Grande's testimony concerns whether the names supplied for verification matched records in the PSA civil-registration database. GMA News reported that Grande acknowledged she could not testify that names appearing in the confidential-fund acknowledgment receipts did or did not belong to real people.

A missing PSA match therefore does not by itself prove that a payee was fictitious. Likewise, where a name matched a deceased person or a minor in PSA records, the match alone does not establish that the person in that civil record was the actual recipient named in the confidential-fund documents.

The prosecution argues that the PSA findings support its allegation of irregular confidential-fund liquidation. Those allegations remain part of an ongoing impeachment trial and have not been adjudicated as proven facts.

sections.heading: Context
paragraphs: Grande testified as a prosecution witness on Article I of the impeachment case, which accuses Duterte of misuse, misappropriation and irregular liquidation of confidential funds under the OVP and DepEd. Duterte served as education secretary from 2022 to 2024 while also serving as vice president.

The prosecution has questioned identities appearing in acknowledgment receipts used to account for confidential-fund expenditures, including the name 'Mary Grace Piattos.' Grande testified that the PSA found no birth, marriage or death record under that name based on the information submitted for verification.

The defense's statement that recipient names were aliases is material because it offers an explanation for why names on the receipts may not correspond to civil-registry identities. Whether the use of aliases was permissible, properly documented or sufficient to answer the prosecution's allegations remains for the parties to argue and the impeachment court to assess.

sections.heading: Why this matters to Filipinos
paragraphs: The testimony concerns accountability for confidential public funds and the evidentiary record in a constitutional proceeding against the sitting vice president. The case could affect public confidence in how confidential funds are documented, audited and overseen across government.

Because impeachment is a political and constitutional trial rather than an ordinary criminal prosecution, individual pieces of evidence should be understood within the full record presented by both the prosecution and defense. FMB News will distinguish testimony, allegations and arguments from findings actually made by the impeachment court.

sections.heading: What to watch next
paragraphs: The prosecution is expected to continue presenting evidence before the defense presents its own case. A central unresolved question is what documentation or testimony the defense will offer to support its position that the names were aliases and how it says the underlying confidential-fund recipients were verified and accounted for.

Readers should also watch for rulings by the impeachment court on the admissibility and weight of the PSA evidence, as well as any official records that clarify how the questioned acknowledgment receipts were prepared, authenticated and audited.

audit.socialCaption: PSA testimony in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial showed no matching civil-registry records for 1,685 of 2,669 names checked from OVP and DepEd confidential-fund payee lists. Duterte's defense says the recipient names were aliases. FMB News explains what the evidence establishes, what it does not prove, and what to watch next.
verificationNotes: The central PSA finding is verified through PNA's direct report of Assistant National Statistician Marizza Grande's testimony and corroborated by GMA News and Philstar.com.
The defense position that recipient names were aliases is independently reported by News5, GMA News and Philstar.com.

The article does not infer that absence of a PSA civil-registry match proves a person was fictitious. GMA News reports that Grande herself said she could not testify whether the names on the receipts did or did not belong to real people.
Matches to records of deceased people or minors are described as name matches rather than proof that those specific people received confidential funds.
The prosecution's misuse allegations are explicitly identified as allegations in an ongoing impeachment trial, not established facts or a finding of guilt.

Repository searches for 'Sara Duterte,' 'confidential funds,' 'Piattos' and 'impeachment trial' did not identify an earlier FMB News article on this specific evidentiary development, so the article is treated as an original report rather than a continuation.
